# I. Ille Ego

Oh, lend me your ear, for I mean to seize
The fire that once burned in Chaucer's breast,
And spin, in mournful verse, if you please,
The tale of Johnny Raw and his quest;

Who, fixed upon some reckless scheme
To set the whole world all agape,
Set off full tilt—no idle dream—
For Hindustan, on Old Poulter's mare.

Tramp! tramp! across the land he sped;
Splash! splash! through ocean's spray;
Then, boastful, raised his voice and said—
"Pray, who could ride as I ride today?

"For I'm the one who dared advance
To rout the ranks of ancient lore,
And swore this mare, by fate or chance,
Was worth what Hector's chargers bore.

"Old Homer, from his throne cast down,
And Virgil struck a mighty blow;
In place of both, without a frown,
I set stout Mother Bunch to go.

"To France I rode upon my roan,
Whose fire and mettle naught could tame;
There, perched upon the tomb of Joan,
I piped a mournful, doleful strain.

"A wild and wondrous song I raised,
To stir my listeners to tears:
But when I looked—struck mute, amazed—
I found them sleeping, deaf to fears!

"Then did I swear a furious oath
To seek some fierce and dire revenge,
And conjured up, to rouse them both,
Stout Taffy with his leek to avenge.

"To Heaven and Hell I rode astray,
Defying wind and stormy weather;
Trumped up a devilish, cursed lay,
And damned them, one and all, together.

"Now, Proteus! Rise, thou shifting seer!
Come, breathe thy spirit in my mare:
In every guise but those appear
Which Taste and Nature justly wear."

# I. He Himself

Listen closely, friends, for now
I'll channel Chaucer's spirit,
And weave in melancholy verse
The story you shall hear it—

Of Johnny Raw, who schemed a plot
So reckless and so bold,
To gallop off toward India
On Poulter's mare, we're told.

Clip-clop! he thundered over land;
Splash-splash! through ocean's spray;
And then he crowed his boastful claim—
"Who rides as well as I, pray?

"For I'm the fellow who set out
To conquer ancient glory,
Declaring this old mare surpassed
Great Hector's steeds in story.

"I knocked old Homer from his perch,
Gave Virgil quite a beating,
And in their honored place installed
Bold Mother Bunch, retreating

"the pair of them to France I dashed
Upon my sturdy roan,
Then perched myself with mournful song
Atop Joan's ancient stone.

"A strange and marvelous tune I sang,
To draw forth every tear:
But glancing up, my voice grew still—
They'd all dozed off, I fear!

"So then I raged a furious curse,
Determined to get even,
And summoned forth, to shake their mirth,
Old Taffy with his leek soon given.

"To Heaven's gate and Hell's own pit
I rode through storm and squall,
Devised a devilish sort of verse,
And damned them one and all.

"Now, shifting Proteus, come forth!
Breathe life into my steed:
Take any form you wish, save those
That Taste and Nature need."

# The Absurd Chronicle of Johnny Raw

The narrator opens with a wry promise to his audience: what follows shall be a tale steeped in mockery and mirth, chronicling the preposterous adventures of one Johnny Raw. This unlikely hero, we are told, sets forth upon a journey of epic pretensions—bound, of all places, for distant Hindoostan—mounted not upon some noble steed but upon Old Poulter's humble mare. Yet humility is nowhere to be found in Johnny's own estimation of the affair. With the swagger of a man utterly convinced of his own magnificence, he boasts to any who will listen that no rider, past or present, could hope to match his equestrian prowess.

Indeed, Johnny's vanity knows no bounds. In a flourish of comic hubris, he declares that his borrowed mare eclipses even the storied horses of Hector, those legendary steeds immortalized in the annals of the Trojan War. Not content with merely rivaling antiquity, Johnny goes further still, casting down the very pillars of classical literature. Homer and Virgil—those twin monarchs of epic verse, long enthroned in the pantheon of human achievement—are unceremoniously toppled from their seats of honor by this self-appointed champion of the absurd.

In their place, Johnny Raw enthrones a figure far removed from the solemn dignity of the ancients: Mother Bunch, that beloved character of English folk tradition, known more for her rustic humor and homespun charm than for any pretension to literary greatness. This substitution is no mere accident of taste but a deliberate act of rebellion—a thumbing of the nose at the lofty standards of classical education and refined culture. Through Mother Bunch, Johnny signals his allegiance to the crude, the comedic, and the common, rejecting outright the polished ideals that generations of scholars had held sacred.

The narrative then carries Johnny across the Channel to France, where his journey takes an unexpectedly theatrical turn. Standing before the tomb of Joan of Arc—a site that might inspire reverence and sorrow in any person of feeling—Johnny attempts a performance of great mournfulness, presumably hoping to move his onlookers to tears with his display of grief. The result, however, is a masterstroke of comic deflation: rather than weeping, his audience has simply drifted off to sleep, utterly unmoved by his theatrical lamentations. The sacred tomb, meant to inspire solemnity, instead becomes the backdrop for an unintentional farce.

This humiliation ignites something fierce in Johnny Raw. Wounded pride gives way to a kind of manic determination, and his subsequent performances spiral into ever more outlandish and diabolical territory. He summons forth Taffy, invokes the powers of both Heaven and Hell, and escalates his theatrical antics to fever pitch, as though sheer volume and spectacle might succeed where genuine emotion had failed. In his final and most desperate gambit, Johnny calls upon Proteus himself—that ancient god of the sea, famed for his ability to shift endlessly between forms. He commands this shape-shifting deity to transform his faithful mare into any conceivable shape or guise, so long as that shape avoids the one thing Johnny seems constitutionally incapable of achieving: genuine Taste and Nature. In this final absurd request, the satire reaches its fullest expression, for Johnny Raw's entire journey has been defined not by authentic artistry but by an endless parade of substitutes, distortions, and comic evasions of true merit.

**THE RIDE OF JOHNNY RAW: A Mock-Heroic Fragment**

*Being a True and Wonderful Account of His Travels upon Old Poulter's Mare, with Digressions into Heaven, Hell, and Sundry Foreign Parts, as Related by Himself to an Audience Increasingly Disinclined to Listen*

---

Sing, Muse—or rather, sing thyself, for I
Am Muse enough, and need no borrowed sky
To lend me wings! Let dusty Homer sleep
In marble halls where critics vainly weep
Over his gaps; let Virgil's stately line
Creak on its hinges—Johnny Raw is mine
To celebrate, and needs no help from Greece
Or Rome, whose heroes travelled but for peace
Or plunder, whilst *my* hero rode astride
A mare of such surpassing bone and hide
That Pegasus himself, were he alive,
Would blush to see how she could kick and thrive.

Old Poulter's mare! No common jade was she,
But knobbed and sprung with strange geometry,
Four legs at least (some say she boasted six
On Tuesdays, when the moon was in a fix),
And Johnny Raw astride her, hat askew,
Cried "Gee!" and off across the world he flew.

First Hindoostan received his clattering hoof;
The natives gaped from many a woven roof
To see a man in gaiters, red of face,
Come thundering through their solemn marketplace,
Demanding curry, tribute, and a throne,
And several elephants to call his own.
"I've seen more wonders," Johnny would declare,
"Than Homer's fellow with the wooden mare
Could dream of in a fortnight!"—here he'd pause
For the applause that never came, because
His listeners, one by one, began to nod,
Their chins upon their chests, their eyelids shod
In heaviness no boasting could dispel;
The tale rolled on, but no one marked it well.

From India next to France the journey ran—
Old Poulter's mare, it seems, ignored the span
Of oceans, mountains, sensible geography,
And galloped straight through Customs, duty-free.
In Paris, Johnny fought a hundred men
(Or was it ten? The number altered when
He told it twice) and dined with kings, and drank
Champagne from goblets of prodigious rank,
And all the while his listeners' heads sank low,
Snoring a counterpoint to his bravado.

But why stop there, when Heaven's gate stood wide?
Old Poulter's mare, undaunted, still could stride
Through pearly portals, past astonished saints
Who dropped their harps at Johnny's loud complaints
That golden streets were paved a trifle rough
For horseshoes, and the manna wasn't enough
To fill a growing hero's hungry frame.
St. Peter, mortified, forgot his name
And waved him through, if only to be rid
Of one who talked so much and never did.

Then, not content, he plunged to regions warm,
Where Pluto's minions, startled by the storm
Of hoofbeats on their sulphurous terrain,
Looked up to see a man with flowing mane
(His own, not hers) come charging through the fire,
Shouting that Virgil's guide—that solemn sire
Who led Aeneas through the shades below—
Had nothing on *his* mare, who feared no glow
Of brimstone, and in fact seemed rather pleased
To find her hooves by devilish heat un-eased
Of certain corns she'd suffered since the spring.
"Aeneas wept," cried Johnny, "at the thing
He saw in Hell—but I have laughed instead,
And bought a bit of pitchfork for my shed!"

And still his listeners slept. One snored so loud
It might have waked the dead within that crowd
Of shades he claimed to've conquered; but in vain—
Not even Hell could rouse the failing brain
Of those who'd heard this tale a hundred times,
Embroidered fresh with more elaborate rhymes,
Yet always ending where it had begun:
With Johnny Raw astride, and no one won
To wonder, save the teller of the tale,
Who never once observed his audience pale
And drooping, but rode on through every land
Upon his mare, his boasting close at hand.

Now, since the truth of this could scarce be told
By common Muse, however free and bold,
I call on Proteus, shifting shape of old,
Who changed to lion, serpent, flame, and flood
To 'scape Menelaus on the Pharian mud—
Come, slippery god, and lend thy changeful arts
Not to disguise plain truth, but wilder parts
Invent! Let Poulter's mare sprout wings of brass,
Let Johnny's hat transform to looking-glass,
Let Hell's own devils learn to knit and sew,
Let Heaven's saints take up the banjo—
For only in such monstrous, gross array
Can Johnny's tale be rightly told today:
Not truth, not art, not taste in any line,
But mere excess, bloated and superfine,
A shape no Proteus, howsoever spry,
Could make more absurd than it stood by.

So ends the ride—or does it? Johnny swore
He'd more to tell, and headed for the door
Of yet another gathering, mare in hand,
To conquer, once again, some sleeping band.

# Ille and Ego: Chaucer's Dialogue with the Divided Self

The terms *Ille* and *Ego*—"He" and "I"—evoke a long tradition of philosophical and literary exploration into the nature of selfhood, a tradition that finds a particularly rich and nuanced expression in the works of Geoffrey Chaucer. While Chaucer never employed these exact Latin terms as a formal framework, the tension they represent—between the observing self and the observed other, between the narrator and the narrated—pervades his poetry in ways that reward careful examination.

Consider the peculiar self-presentation Chaucer constructs throughout his major works. In *The Canterbury Tales*, the pilgrim "Chaucer" who narrates the journey is himself a curious hybrid: both author and character, both *Ego* (the writing consciousness shaping the narrative) and *Ille* (the bumbling, rather foolish pilgrim who tells the dreadfully dull *Tale of Sir Thopas*). This split allows Chaucer remarkable freedom. As *Ego*, he can craft sophisticated ironies and orchestrate complex narrative structures; as *Ille*, he can feign naivety, disclaim responsibility for bawdy content, and present himself as merely a reporter of others' words rather than their author.

This doubling appears even more explicitly in *Troilus and Criseyde*, where the narrator repeatedly steps back from his own story, claiming only to translate or transmit a tale that exists independently of his shaping hand. The narrator becomes *Ille*—a mere vessel—even as the poem's exquisite structure reveals the unmistakable presence of *Ego*, the controlling artistic intelligence.

This dynamic reflects broader medieval concerns with authorship, authority, and the relationship between the writing self and the written persona. Chaucer inherited from classical and medieval rhetorical traditions an awareness that the "I" of a text is always, to some degree, a construction—a mask (*persona*) distinct from the historical individual holding the pen. Yet unlike purely conventional uses of this device, Chaucer exploits the *Ille/Ego* tension for genuine philosophical and comic effect, using the gap between his two selves to explore questions of truth, fiction, judgment, and moral responsibility.

The result is a body of work in which selfhood itself becomes provisional and multiple—where the "I" who writes and the "he" who is written about exist in productive, illuminating tension.

# THE JOLLY RIDE OF JOHNNY RAW
### *A Burlesque Romaunt, in the Manner of the Ancient Canterburie Tales*

**Prologue**

Whan that Apryl with his shoures swote
(Or, plainly speaking, when the roads were wet),
And every alehouse-keeper kept his note
Of debts that jolly topers would forget,
Then Johnny Raw, a hero staunch and stout,
Did buckle on his boots and sally out
Upon a mare of controversial worth,
To seek his fortune round the parish-earth.

**Fitt the First: Of Johnny and His Steed**

This Johnny was no knight of high renown,
No paladin with pennon, lance, or crest;
His only armour was a fustian gown,
His only weapon was a walking-jest.
Yet in his soul there burned as fierce a fire
As ever moved Sir Lancelot or his sire,
For he had vowed—by pipe and pot of beer—
To win the hand of Polly Prue, his dear.

His mare (yclept Grimalkin, for her spite)
Was lean as Lent, and stubborn as a mule;
She had one eye for glory, one for flight,
And judged all riders by a single rule:
To go where they would *not*, with all her heart,
And stop, stone-still, whenever they would start.
Yet Johnny, mounted, cried with visage bold,
"Now, Dobbin"—wrong her name, but never told—
"On! On to Polly, though the road be long,
And Fame shall pipe the burden of my song!"

**Fitt the Second: The Peril of the Pigsty**

Now on their way a peril soon they met:
A pigsty, breach'd, with grunters ranging free,
Who, seeing Johnny's steed so gaunt and wet,
Did charge him as if bent on victory.
Then might you well have seen, in that same hour,
A mock Achilles meet a mock Hector's power—
For Johnny, brandishing his oaken stave,
Cried "Yield, base swine!"—as valiant knights should rave—
While good Grimalkin, terror in her breast,
Bolted, and left her master to the rest.

Full sore beset, amid the muddy roar,
He fought (or fled) as heroes do in tales—
That is to say, he tumbled on the floor,
And measured, with his person, all the vales
Of that unhappy sty; yet rose again,
Bespattered, but (thank Heaven) not in pain,
And, mounting once more on Grimalkin's back,
Pursued, undaunted, his triumphant track.

**Fitt the Third: The Winning of Fair Polly**

At length he reached the cottage of his fair,
Who, spying him bemired from top to toe,
Did nearly swoon for laughter, then and there—
But love, dear reader, conquers even so.
For Polly, seeing how he'd dared the swine
And ridden forth on such a beast as mine
(Grimalkin, I should say, and not the pig),
Did deem him worthy, mud and all, and big
Enough in heart, whatever small in state,
To be her champion, and to share her gate.

**L'Envoy**

Thus endeth, gentles, my burlesque so brief,
Of Johnny Raw, his mare, and muddy grief.
Let Homer sing of Troy, and Chaucer tell
Of knights who battled to be loved so well—
I sing of him who, mounted on a hack,
Fell in a sty, and gallantly came back;
For true it is, in love as well as war,
'Tis not the steed, but *heart*, that wins the door.

counterfactuals.output:
**THE BALLAD OF SIR BRAGGADOCIO**

Sir Braggadocio rode to town
Upon a spavined mare,
His helm was tin, his sword was wood,
But mighty was his air.

"I've heard," quoth he to the tavern folk,
"Of Hector, prince of Troy—
A puling knave who wept for home,
A mother's whimpering boy!

"Had *I* stood forth on Ilium's wall
When Achilles came to blows,
I'd not have run three circuits round—
I'd have punched him on the nose!"

The alewife poured his cup of sack,
The children gathered near,
And Braggadocio puffed his chest
And drank his fill of beer.

"As for blind Homer, that old fraud,
Who sang of ships and spears—
He never saw a battle fought!
(He hadn't any *eyes*, m'dears!)

"I'd wager that if I had lived
When Troy's tall towers burned,
I'd fix the whole affair in verse
Far better than he learned!

"And Virgil, too, that Roman scribe
Who sent poor Dido mad—
He made his hero flee the fire
And called the coward *good*!

Had I been steering Trojan ships
I'd not have jilted her—
I'd not have needed gods to shove
Me off—I'd not have stirred!"

Now as he bragged, a stranger came,
Cloaked all in dusty grey,
Who smiled to hear such mighty words
And softly bid him: "Stay—

"For I am bound to Bosworth Field
Come morning, with the King,
And thou, who mock'st the ancient dead,
Shalt taste of soldiering."

Sir Braggadocio's face went pale
As parchment, thin and old.
"I—er—recall a pressing task,
A debt, unpaid, in gold—"

But dawn came on, and drums did roll,
And trumpets called the men,
And Braggadocio, green as grass,
Was mounted up again.

He did not charge. He did not fight.
He hid behind a bush,
And when the battle's roar died down
They found him in the rush—

His wooden sword still in its sheath,
His tin helm dinted not,
For he had spent the whole affair
A-cowering on the spot.

So here's the moral of my song,
Ye braggarts, mark it well:
'Tis easier to mock the brave
Than share the tale they tell.

For Hector died with honor's shield,
And Homer sang the truth,
And Braggadocio ran away—
And that's the whole, in sooth.

**The Tale of Sir Bumbleton the Bold**

Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote  
Had wet the roade beneathe my horse's foote,  
Then forth I rode, a knyght of muche renowne  
(Or so I tolde eche wenche in every towne).

"I am," quod I, "as bold as Hercules,  
And smarter yet than all the Socrateses!  
Sir Lancelot were but a pageboy to my grace,  
And Alexandre wepte to see my face!"

My steede, a swaybacked nag of dubious yeeres,  
Did fart and stumble, pricking up his eares,  
As if to saye, "Good sire, thou talkest wynde—  
Thou hast no swoord, no shield, no sense combyned!"

Yet on I rode from Engelond to Fraunce,  
Proclaiming loud my prowess and my staunce,  
"I am the sonne of Zeus!" I telle the Frenche,  
Who onlye laugh and offre me a wrenche

To fixe my horse, whose leg had gone quite lame  
From all my boastes and pompous, empty fame.  
Through Spainne I went, and calde myself El Cid,  
The peasants asked, "Then wherefore dost thou kid?

Thou hast no armee, and thy horse doth wheeze,  
Thou smellest worse than week-old Belgian cheese!"  
Yet still I sang my songe of derring-do,  
Through mountain, bog, and Alpine avenue,

Comparing me to Caesar, Cid, and Cain  
(The laste I chose in error, to my shame),  
Til in Romania a farmer sayde,  
"Good sir, thy legend is but poorly made—

Thou art no hero, but a pompous foole  
Who ridest forth on ass, not stallion coole!"  
And so I learned, thoughe late, this lesson true:  
'Tis better to be humble than a fool who crew

Of gods and kings while riding but a mule—  
Yet still, methinks, I'll call myself "the Jewel  
of Christendom," and ride on anywaye,  
For legends, friends, are made of what men saye!

**The Geste of Sir Wobblesnout, Knight of the Pudding**

Hark, hark, ye gentles, gather near,
And lend a lobe, and lend an ear,
For I shall sing, in minstrel's mode,
Of quests absurd on England's road.

'Twas not for grail nor golden fleece
Our hero rode, but for goose-grease,
A pudding stol'n from cook's own pot—
This was his cause, his knightly lot!

He donned his helm (a colander),
And cried, "By Joan of Arc, I swear!
As she did rout the English horde,
So I shall smite with wooden sword!"

Then down the lane came Taffy true,
His leek held high, his boots askew,
Quoth he, "Good sir, I'll join thy quest,
For leeks and puddings both taste best!"

Together rode this comic pair,
Through bog and briar, hill and lair,
Till at a stream, both dark and deep,
They met a shape that seemed to creep—

'Twas Proteus, old shifting sprite,
Who turned to eel, then wolf, then kite,
"None catch me!" laughed he, wild and free,
"I am the riddle of the sea!"

But Taffy swung his leek so bold,
It caught the god in fishy hold,
"Enough!" cried Proteus, turned to man,
"Here's thy lost pudding—take it, an
You'll let me back into my stream,
I'll trouble you no more, I deem!"

So home they went, our knight and friend,
Their farcical quest brought to its end,
With pudding warm and leek in hand—
The greatest heroes in the land!

So raise a cup, ye listeners all,
To Joan, to Taffy, great and small,
To Proteus too, that slippery elf—
Sing hey the day! Sing ho thyself!

**THE BOASTFUL CAVALIER: A Monologue Delivered With Excessive Confidence**

Pray, gather round, ye scholars pale, ye bards of dusty tome,
And I shall spin a truer tale than ever left old Homer's home!
That blind Greek fool, with lyre in hand, sang of a horse of wood—
A hollow trick! A carpenter's prank! I'd not call *that* thing good.

But *I*, dear friends, have ridden forth on Nell, my speckled mare,
Whose hooves strike sparks from solid cloud and part the very air!
No wooden horse concealed with men crept sneaking through a gate—
My Nell doth *fly*, and breathe out steam, and thinks the wind's too late!

Let Jason keep his Golden Fleece, his Argo, and his crew,
I found a sheep with silver wool while pausing for a stew.
I clipped its back with pocket shears, made mittens for my hands,
And rode on home by teatime to the wonderment of lands!

Aeneas fled from burning Troy with father on his back—
I carried *both* my in-laws once, and never felt the lack!
Through fire, flood, and one bad tavern where the ale was thin,
I bore them nobly on my mare and only slightly grinned.

Bellerophon, that showy chap, on Pegasus did soar—
But *his* horse needed wings, forsooth! Mine needs not even more
Than a suggestion, whispered soft, of "Nellie, let us fly"—
She rises like a soufflé does, and we are in the sky!

Alexander wept, they say, with no more worlds to take,
I wept but once—when Nell and I fell in a treacle lake.
We conquered continents by lunch, made peace with several kings,
And still got home in time to hear the supper-summoning rings.

So let the ancient poets speak of heroes bold and grand,
Of monsters slain and cities burned and journeys nobly planned—
I'll match them all, and better still, for I have something rare:
The wit to boast about it *and* a genuinely flying mare.

Now pour the wine and raise a toast, ye skeptical and shy—
For legends fade to modesty, but *I* shall never die
Of understatement, nor of doubt, nor humbleness's blight—
Come, Nellie! To the moon and back! We've plans to make tonight!
